messages.text: 好，那我想問一下，這篇論文裡面的「fun」到底是由什麼組成的？是不是就是遊戲的規則和目標？

messages.short_answer: 論文的檢索段落中並沒有明確把「fun」定義為一個獨立概念。MDA 的三個核心部分是 Mechanics、Dynamics 和 Aesthetics，其中 Aesthetics 指玩家與遊戲系統互動時產生的理想情緒反應，最接近你說的「fun」。所以「fun」不等於規則和目標本身：規則屬於 Mechanics，會透過 Dynamics 產生 Aesthetics 體驗。目前找到的段落不足以確認論文如何直接定義 fun。

sections.title: 三層之間的關係
sections.text: 論文說 Mechanics 是遊戲在資料表示與演算法層面的組成部分，Dynamics 是這些機制在執行時、面對玩家輸入與彼此輸出時的行為，Aesthetics 則是玩家與系統互動時被引發的理想情緒反應。從設計者角度看，機制產生動態系統行為，進而帶來特定的美學體驗。

sections.title: 為什麼規則不等於 fun
sections.text: 可以把規則和目標理解為設計的起點，而 fun 更像玩家在遊玩過程中實際感受到的結果。論文的框架是從規則出發，經過系統運作，最後落在玩家的情緒體驗上，因此規則是必要條件之一，但不是 fun 本身。

sections.title: 一個假設性的例子
sections.text: （此例不是論文內容）假設一款遊戲的規則是「跳躍會消耗體力」。在不同關卡中，玩家會因為體力管理而產生節奏感或緊張感，這些動態互動才可能讓玩家覺得有趣。

sources.text:
The difference between games and other entertainment products (such as books, music, movies and plays) is that their consumption is relatively unpredictable. The string of events that occur during gameplay and the outcome of those events are unknown at the time the product is finished.

The MDA framework formalizes the consumption of games by breaking them into their distinct components:

...and establishing their design counterparts:

Mechanics describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.

Dynamics describes the run-time behavior of the mechanics acting on player inputs and each others’ outputs over time.

Aesthetics describes the desirable emotional responses evoked in the player, when she interacts with the game system.

Fundamental to this framework is the idea that games are more like artifacts than media. By this we mean that the content of a game is its behavior – not the media that streams out of it towards the player.
quotes: Aesthetics describes the desirable emotional responses evoked in the player, when she interacts with the game system.
Mechanics describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.

sources.text:
Thinking about games as designed artifacts helps frame them as systems that build behavior via interaction. It supports clearer design choices and analysis at all levels of study and development. MDA in Detail MDA as Lens Each component of the MDA framework can be thought of as a “lens” or a “view” of the game – separate, but causally linked. [LeBlanc, 2004b].

From the designer’s perspective, the mechanics give rise to dynamic system behavior, which in turn leads to particular aesthetic experiences. From the player’s perspective, aesthetics set the tone, which is born out in observable dynamics and eventually, operable mechanics.

When working with games, it is helpful to consider both the designer and player perspectives. It helps us observe how even small changes in one layer can cascade into others. In addition, thinking about the player encourages experience-driven (as opposed to feature-driven) design.

messages.text: 那第二個（Dynamics）是不是就是遊戲跑起來之後的情況？可以舉個例子嗎？我還是有點抽象。

messages.short_answer: 你的理解大致正確。Dynamics 指的是 Mechanics 在遊戲運行時的行為，它會隨時間作用於玩家的輸入，以及系統元件彼此的輸出，也就是遊戲跑起來後實際表現出來的互動過程。

sections.title: 論文如何定義 Dynamics
sections.text: 論文指出 Dynamics 描述 Mechanics 在運行時的行為，作用於玩家輸入以及彼此的輸出，並且隨時間展開。Mechanics 是資料表示與演算法層面的組成，Dynamics 則是這些組成在執行時的表現。

sections.title: 用白話理解：規則本身與規則跑起來的過程
sections.text: 可以把 Mechanics 想成寫好的規則，例如「被擊中會扣血」。Dynamics 則是遊戲進行中，玩家攻擊、對手反應、血量逐漸下降後，整體形成的互動局面。前者是靜態設計，後者是執行中的過程。

sections.title: 假設性例子：限時對戰遊戲
sections.text: 假設規則是「每局限時三分鐘，時間到就比分數」。玩家一開始可能穩健累積分數，但剩下三十秒時對手開始冒險搶分，雙方不斷互相回應。這種由時間限制與對手行為交錯而產生的緊張局面，就是 Dynamics 的運行情況（此例為說明用，並非論文內容）。

sections.title: 論文中的相關說明：挑戰感從何而來
sections.text: 論文舉例說，挑戰感是由時間壓力和對手的遊戲行為等因素產生。這說明 Dynamics 如何支撐 Aesthetics 中的體驗，而不只是規則本身。

It’s easy to see that supporting adversarial play and clear feedback about who is winning are essential to competitive games. If the player doesn’t see a clear winning condition, or feels like they can’t possibly win, the game is suddenly a lot less interesting. Dynamic Models Dynamics work to create aesthetic experiences. For example, challenge is created by things like time pressure and opponent play. Fellowship can be encouraged by sharing information across certain members of a session (a team) or supplying winning c onditions that are more difficult to achieve alone (such as capturing an enemy base).

Expression comes from dynamics that encourage individual users to leave their mark: systems for purchasing, building or earning game items, for designing, constructing and changing le vels or worlds, and for creating personalized, unique characters . Dramatic tension comes from dynamics that en courage a rising tension, a release, and a denouement.

messages.text: 好，我現在比較懂 Dynamics 了。所以我的理解是：設計者是先想好 Mechanics，然後玩家也是照著這個順序一步一步體驗，先碰到機制，再有動態，最後才感受到 Aesthetics，跟設計者的順序一樣對吧？那這樣是不是代表玩家其實也是從規則開始理解遊戲的？

messages.short_answer: 這個理解只對了一半。論文描述的是兩個視角的方向相反：設計者從 Mechanics 出發，經 Dynamics 產生 Aesthetics；玩家則是從 Aesthetics 開始，再透過可觀察的 Dynamics 回到 Mechanics。所以不能說玩家也是照設計者的順序從規則開始理解遊戲。

sections.title: 論文中的兩個方向
sections.text: 論文先從設計者的角度說明 Mechanics 產生動態系統行為，進而帶來特定的審美體驗；再從玩家的角度說明 Aesthetics 先設定基調，然後在可觀察的 Dynamics 中體現，最後才是可操作的 Mechanics。

sections.title: 用白話說方向的差異
sections.text: 可以把它想成同一條鏈的兩個讀法：設計者是「規則 → 行為 → 感受」，玩家的感受先出現，然後才回頭去察覺行為與規則。兩者關注的層次相同，但起點和推進方向不同。

sections.title: 這段論文沒有證明的部分
sections.text: 段落描述的是兩種視角的框架，並沒有研究真實玩家如何逐步學習或體驗遊戲，因此不能據此推斷玩家實際上是否先理解規則。若你想確認玩家的認知順序，需要其他研究或實證資料。

messages.text: 那我想到上課的例子：老師說有一款遊戲機制很多、功能也很多，但玩起來還是很無聊。這跟論文的三層架構有關嗎？如果機制都有，為什麼還是不好玩？

messages.short_answer: 論文的架構支持「機制多不代表好玩」這個看法：機制先產生 Dynamics（執行時的動態行為），再引出 Aesthetics（玩家的情緒體驗），中間任何一層沒有接好，都可能讓玩家覺得無聊。論文也明說沒有公式能決定哪些元素組合會產生「fun」。不過，段落中沒有直接討論老師舉的「機制很多但無聊」案例。

sections.title: 三層之間的因果鏈
sections.text: 論文說，從設計者的角度看，機制會產生動態系統行為，進而帶來特定的美學體驗。論文也強調各層之間是因果相連的，小的改變可能沿著層次一路影響到其他層。

sections.title: 為什麼機制多不等於好玩
sections.text: 依照這個因果鏈，機制數量只是起點；如果它們在執行時產生的動態沒有支持玩家想要的情緒體驗，就可能出現老師說的情況。這是我根據論文架構做的推論，論文本身沒有討論「無聊」。

sections.title: 論文對「fun」的態度
sections.text: 論文指出每款遊戲會追求多種美學目標，程度不一，並且承認沒有能決定哪些元素組合會產生「fun」的公式。這表示論文並不提供一套保證有趣的配方。

retrieved.text: In this paper we present the MDA framework (standing for Mechanics, Dynamics, and Aesthetics), developed and taught as part of the Game Design and Tuning Workshop at the Game Developers Conference, San Jose 2001-2004 [LeBlanc, 2004a]. MDA is a formal approach to understanding games – one which attempts to bridge the gap between game design and development, game criticism, and technical game research. We believe this methodology will clarify and strengthen the iterative processes of developers, scholars and researchers alike, making it easier for all parties to decompose, study and design a broad class of game designs and game artifacts. Towards a Comprehensive Framework Game design and authorship happen at many levels, and the fields of games research and development involve people from diverse creative and scholarly backgrounds. While it’s often necessary to focus on one area, everyone, regardless of discipline, will at some point need to consider issues outside that area: base mechanisms of game systems, the overarching design goals, or the desired experiential results of gameplay.

Thinking about games as designed artifacts helps frame them as systems that build behavior via interaction. It supports clearer design choices and analysis at all levels of study and development. MDA in Detail MDA as Lens Each component of the MDA framework can be thought of as a “lens” or a “view” of the game – separate, but causally linked. [LeBlanc, 2004b].

From the designer’s perspective, the mechanics give rise to dynamic system behavior, which in turn leads to particular aesthetic experiences. From the player’s perspective, aesthetics set the tone, which is born out in observable dynamics and eventually, operable mechanics.

When working with games, it is helpful to consider both the designer and player perspectives. It helps us observe how even small changes in one layer can cascade into others. In addition, thinking about the player encourages experience-driven (as opposed to feature-driven) design.

The difference between games and other entertainment products (such as books, music, movies and plays) is that their consumption is relatively unpredictable. The string of events that occur during gameplay and the outcome of those events are unknown at the time the product is finished.

The MDA framework formalizes the consumption of games by breaking them into their distinct components:

...and establishing their design counterparts:

Mechanics describes the particular components of the game, at the level of data representation and algorithms.

Dynamics describes the run-time behavior of the mechanics acting on player inputs and each others’ outputs over time.

Aesthetics describes the desirable emotional responses evoked in the player, when she interacts with the game system.

Fundamental to this framework is the idea that games are more like artifacts than media. By this we mean that the content of a game is its behavior – not the media that streams out of it towards the player.

hunicke@cs.northwestern.edu, marc_leblanc@alum.mit.edu, rob@cs.northwestern.edu

Abstract In this paper we present the MDA framework (standing for Mechanics, Dynamics, and Aesthetics), developed and taught as part of the Game Design and Tuning Workshop at the Game Developers Conference, San Jose 2001-2004.

MDA is a formal approach to understanding games – one which attempts to bridge th e gap between game design and development, game criticism, and technical game research. We believe this methodology will clarify and strengthen the iterative processes of develope rs, scholars and researchers alike, making it easier for all parties to decompose, study and design a broad class of game designs and game artifacts.

Introduction All artifacts are created within some design methodology. Whether building a physical prototype, architecting a software interface, constructing an argument or implementing a series of controlled experiments – design methodologies guide the creative thought process and help ensure quality work.

MDA supports a formal, iterative approach to design and tuning. It allows us to reas on explicitly about particular design goals, and to anticipate how changes will impact each aspect of the framework and the resulting designs/implementations.

By moving between MDA’s three levels of abstraction, we can conceptualize the dynamic behavior of game systems. Understanding games as dynamic systems helps us develop techniques for iterative design and improvement – allowing us to control for undesired outcomes, and tune for desired behavior.

In addition, by understanding how formal decisions about gameplay impact the end user experience, we are able to better decompose that experience, and use it to fuel new designs, research and criticism respectively. References Barwood, H. & Falstein, N. 2002. “More of the 400: Discovering Design Rules”. Lecture at Game Developers Conference, 2002. Available online at: http://www.gdconf.com/archives/2002/hal_barwood.ppt

Church, D. 1999. “Formal Abstract Design Tools.” Game Developer, August 1999. San Francisco, CA: CMP Media. Available online at: http://www.gamasutra.com/features/19990716/design_tool s_01.htm

AI coders and researchers are no exception. Seemingly inconsequential decisions about data, representation, algorithms, tools, vocabulary and methodology will trickle upward, shaping the final gameplay. Similarly, all desired user experience must bottom out, somewhere, in code. As games continue to generate increasingly complex agent, object and system behavior, AI and game design merge.

Systematic coherence comes when conflicting constraints are satisfied, and each of the game’s parts can relate to each other as a whole. D ecomposing, understanding and creating this coherence requires travel between all levels of abstraction – fluent motion from systems and code, to content and play experience, and back.

persona_text:
# Persona: Mei

**Who.** Mei is a third-year undergraduate from Taiwan taking a game design course, and a non-native
English speaker. A topic from the lecture caught her interest, so she is reading the teacher's extra
readings on her own.

**What she wants.** To understand the main ideas well enough to explain them and connect them to the
lecture. She has no research project. Reading goal: *Get a general overview of this paper*.

**How she behaves.**
- Writes in Traditional Chinese (繁體字). Interface language: 中文（繁體）.
- Has limited background. Starts with broad questions ("這篇在講什麼？"), then asks for basic definitions.
- Often restates an idea in her own words to check her understanding, and is sometimes wrong (e.g. mixes up
  mechanics and dynamics, or treats a game mechanic as the same thing as a rule or a goal).
- Says plainly when she still does not understand ("還是不太懂", "可以換個方式解釋嗎？").
- Tends to accept answers and rarely opens the sources unless prompted.
- Brings in examples from games she plays or from the lecture and asks whether they fit the paper.

**Papers.** MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research; Game Studies – Defining Game Mechanics.

You are role-playing a learner who is reading an academic paper with PaperLens, a conversational reading
tool. Stay in character as the persona below for the whole conversation.

<persona>
{persona}
</persona>

Situation
- Paper: {paper_title}
- Reading goal chosen in PaperLens: {reading_goal}
- Research context the learner typed into PaperLens: {research_context}

Your task each turn
- Write ONLY the learner's next chat message, as the persona would type it into a chat box.
- Carry out the move given for this turn, adapted naturally to what PaperLens has just said. The move says
  WHAT the learner does; you decide the exact wording in the persona's voice.
- If the move asks you to state a misunderstanding, state it confidently as your own understanding; do not
  hint that it is wrong.
- If the move asks you to refer back to something, use a short reference ("that", "the second one",
  "你刚才说的那个") instead of repeating the full term, exactly as a real learner would.
- Use the persona's language and writing style. Keep the message short (usually 1-3 sentences).
- Base what you say about the paper only on what PaperLens has told you so far; you have not read the paper
  yourself beyond that.
- Never mention that you are simulated, never describe the move, and never evaluate PaperLens.

log.instruction: Ask what the paper says 'fun' is made of.
log.learner_message: 好，那我想問一下，這篇論文裡面的「fun」到底是由什麼組成的？是不是就是遊戲的規則和目標？

log.instruction: Refer to 'the second kind' with a short reference and ask for an example.
log.learner_message: 那第二個（Dynamics）是不是就是遊戲跑起來之後的情況？可以舉個例子嗎？我還是有點抽象。

log.instruction: State a misunderstanding: you think players experience mechanics first and aesthetics last, the same as designers.
log.learner_message: 好，我現在比較懂 Dynamics 了。所以我的理解是：設計者是先想好 Mechanics，然後玩家也是照著這個順序一步一步體驗，先碰到機制，再有動態，最後才感受到 Aesthetics，跟設計者的順序一樣對吧？那這樣是不是代表玩家其實也是從規則開始理解遊戲的？

log.instruction: Ask how this connects to a lecture example where a game was boring even though it had many features.
log.learner_message: 那我想到上課的例子：老師說有一款遊戲機制很多、功能也很多，但玩起來還是很無聊。這跟論文的三層架構有關嗎？如果機制都有，為什麼還是不好玩？

log.instruction: Ask whether the authors give a concrete game as an example in the paper.
log.learner_message: 那論文裡面有沒有用一款具體的遊戲來當例子？我想找一個比較實際的，可以拿來跟老師上課講的內容對照。
